- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

=== case-study--fast-friday-flip-from-friday-walkthrough.md
source: "QLdbKUiNadg, SSAC18, Preparing for the Game Optimizing Player Performance"
---
# Case Study: Moving the Fast Session From Thursday to Friday at Kentucky
**What it is** — Morris describes one program's in-season change (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36]).
- **Before:** Monday to Wednesday practice, Thursday the faster practice, Friday a complete walkthrough, Saturday game. With an evening Saturday game that left "48 hours potentially 72 hours" with little central-nervous-system or bioenergetic stimulus, and athletes "ended up coming out flat" (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]).
- **Change:** a "fast Friday", keeping intensity on Friday while volume stays low.
- **Reported effect:** "our readiness will go you know through the roof both subjectively and objectively on game day"; the heart rate variability device ("mega wave", caption spelling) had shifted more parasympathetic under the old pattern, and subjective wellness rose on Saturday after the flip (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36], [17:07]).
- **Measures:** wellness questionnaires plus a heart rate variability wearable, with the explicit caveat that heart rate variability gives "good things and bad things" (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05]).
- **Linemen detail:** linemen "don't do anything on Fridays" and the Friday drop is their lowest day, so they need the stimulation as much as the skill players (QLdbKUiNadg [13:58]). Skill players target about 75% of game high-speed distance in the week (QLdbKUiNadg [13:27]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a long gap with no stimulation leaves the nervous system and energy systems flat for the game (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]). No data or test of that mechanism is given. Inference: it could also be that the athletes simply feel better with a familiar-intensity day, which the talk cannot separate.
**When to apply** — As an option to examine for evening or late-kickoff games where hard work ends three days out. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15) describes Baylor's game week as Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice with a lighter lift Wednesday, and "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game". Inference: the rule of ending hard work 72 hours out and the Fast Friday pattern are different designs, and this talk cannot decide between them. Eric's baseline: Eric's own SportSmith writing states that subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes learned to game them (`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`), so the subjective half of this evidence is the half he has distrusted.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one team's own change, no control, no numbers shown for the readiness changes, and no result on performance or injury. The speaker reports mixed value of heart rate variability. Wellness scores are subjective. Do not cite as evidence that Friday intensity improves game performance. Do not copy it into a Baylor week without Athletic Performance and the head coach, because it conflicts with the 72-hour rule above.
**Example** — The talk's own sequence: Thursday fast day plus Friday walkthrough replaced by Friday fast day, then readiness read from wellness and heart rate variability on Saturday (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36]).
**Related** — [[claim--alactic-detraining-if-stimulated-only-on-game-day]], [[heuristic--hold-volume-raise-intensity-trim-low-value-periods]]; existing library: [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] (Issurin; the same logic of cutting volume while keeping maximal-speed and specific work before competition).

=== claim--alactic-detraining-if-stimulated-only-on-game-day.md
source: "QLdbKUiNadg, SSAC18, Preparing for the Game Optimizing Player Performance"

# If the Alactic System Is Stimulated Only on Saturday, It May Detrain: A Five-to-Eight-Day Rule of Thumb
**What it is** — Morris says that "from a physiologist standpoint" an energy system "responsible for a lactic power" (caption spelling; context says alactic) is lost if it is not stimulated "every five to eight days", so a lineman who only does game-like work on Saturday "was potentially detraining across the season" (QLdbKUiNadg [08:47]). He classifies the lineman's work as alactic: efforts of about 8 seconds, "anything less than ten all-out", repeated, with a work-to-rest ratio of about 1 to 3.75 (QLdbKUiNadg [10:50], [11:21]). The assertion is stated as a general fact with no citation.
**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no source for the five-to-eight-day figure. Inference: it is a detraining (loss of a trained quality without re-exposure) argument, and it sits in the same range as Issurin's residual duration for maximum speed (alactic), 5 ± 3 days, in the existing library entry below. Issurin's table is about a different population and different quality (maximal speed), so this is a similarity, not a confirmation.
**When to apply** — As a planning prompt: check when, in the week, each position group gets its most game-like, brief, all-out exposure. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15) describes the in-season game week as heavy lift Monday, heavy practice Tuesday and Wednesday, and lifting and hard practice ending 72 hours before a Saturday game.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: an assertion with no data shown. The talk measures contact load in practice versus game but never measures loss of alactic capacity, so "potentially detraining" is a hypothesis about Kentucky's linemen. Do not read the range as an Issurin-style tested figure for line play. It applies to a quality (repeated alactic power efforts) that the speaker says matches an 8-second play, and it should not be extended to other energy systems.
**Example** — Inference: a line group that has a speed or short-effort exposure Tuesday and Wednesday but only walkthroughs after that goes about 72 hours with no all-out work before a Saturday game; that is the pattern the speaker worries about (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]).
**Related** — [[claim--lineman-practice-contact-load-well-below-game]], [[case-study--fast-friday-flip-from-friday-walkthrough]]; existing library: [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] (Issurin), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] (Issurin).

# Linemen and Wide Receivers Reach Similar Player Load by Very Different Routes
**What it is** — Morris says that in the team's game data, offensive linemen and wide receivers have "very similar" total player load, but what makes up that load differs: the linemen have much lower explosive yardage, high-speed distance and max speed (QLdbKUiNadg [03:34], [04:04]). The speaker defines player load as "a summation" of movement from the unit, "a really really really fancy Fitbit" (QLdbKUiNadg [03:34]). The speaker compares the two to "MIT culture versus Booker's" (caption wording, garbled; "bookers" is described as a high-alcohol bourbon): both reach the same point, "it depends on how you get there" (QLdbKUiNadg [05:06]). No numbers are read aloud.
**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the observation that linemen "bang all day" while receivers are running (QLdbKUiNadg [05:06]). Inference: player load adds up all movement, so a contact-heavy, short-burst profile and a running-heavy profile can sum to the same value.
**When to apply** — As a warning when one number is used across positions. Eric's baseline: "Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands" (Explicit, baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13). Inference: a team-wide player-load target or a coach's comparison of "who worked harder" can mislead if the make-up is not checked, and position-level splits can be read next to player load.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the figures are not stated in the audio, so the size of "very similar" and "very different" cannot be checked. One team, two position groups (the talk does not say how many games or seasons). Do not read it as showing that player load is a poor metric, which the speaker does not claim.
**Example** — The talk's own case: an offensive line coach threw the speaker's report in the trash, which spurred slicing each play to see what the load consisted of (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04], [04:34]).
**Related** — [[framework--slice-plays-and-count-contacts-to-define-lineman-game-demand]], [[heuristic--show-coaches-and-athletes-the-data-in-their-terms]].

=== claim--fewer-than-one-percent-of-plays-reach-90-percent-max-speed.md
source: "QLdbKUiNadg, SSAC18, Preparing for the Game Optimizing Player Performance"

# In Over 1,000 Plays From One Season, Fewer Than 1% Reached 90% of a Player's Max Speed
**What it is** — Morris reports that of "over the thousand plays" he broke down from the previous season, "less than 1%" at "any position" reached 90% of that player's max velocity (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). On an average lineman play, travel was 13.5 yards, with direction "25% to the left 25% to the right" (garbled caption: "change direction and art plays 25% to the left"; QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). His conclusion: football is "a game of acceleration" more than of top speed, because a player seldom gets 20 to 30 yards without contact or a change of direction (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). He says this was "shocking" to the head coach and the strength coach, "all about speed" (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). The slide's position breakdown is not captioned, and "the big" is the group he specifies for the 13.5-yard figure ("for our big specifically", QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]).
**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker: short distances, contact and direction changes cut off the chance to build speed (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). Nothing beyond that is given. Inference: because the metric is a percent of each player's own max, a fast player's 90% is a higher absolute speed than a slow player's, so this is a statement about exposure to near-max effort per player, not about absolute mph.
**When to apply** — When deciding how much of a position's practice or conditioning should be spent at near-max velocity versus accelerating and decelerating. Check it against Baylor's own game files per position group before acting. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary" (Explicit, gap, stated as a gap); Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Inference: Morris's count is about game exposure to near-max speed, whereas the Issurin point is about how long a trained quality persists; they answer different questions and the combination is not tested in this talk.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: a single program and one season, described by the speaker without a stated method for how 90% of max was computed; the number of plays is only "over a thousand", position and level of play (Kentucky's college offense) are not broken down in the audio. It does not show that max-speed training is unimportant: it shows a low frequency of 90% exposures in games. A player who does reach 90% in a play may still decide that play. The captions run together "90% of their max" with an unclear phrase ("max B"), so treat the exact metric as caption-garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). Existing library entries on the Harries AFL cohort set the max-velocity decision gates at 75-85% and above 90%, so the cut point here is a convention, not a threshold with evidence.
**Example** — From the talk: the strength coach built around speed, while the 1,000-play breakdown showed almost no play at 90% of max (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]).
**Related** — [[framework--slice-plays-and-count-contacts-to-define-lineman-game-demand]]; existing library: [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]], [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]] (Harries; agreement that the percent-of-max frame is used, different purpose), [[claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion]].

# Kentucky's Linemen Averaged 1.54 Load per Contact in Their Hardest Practice Against 2.22 in Games
**What it is** — Morris compared practice to game using the line metric. His reported figures:

# Define a Lineman's Game Demand by Slicing Each Play and Counting Contacts, Then Train Backwards From It

Step 2: a published study from "a group at the University of Michigan" (a paper he places at about last year) reported about 3,600 yards of game distance, but Morris says that figure is load, not the demands of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [01:32], [03:04]). Step 3: upload every game file to OpenField (Catapult's analytics platform) and "slice each individual play" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). Step 4: use Catapult's offensive-line metric. A gyroscope in the unit recognizes when the lineman drops into his stance, which marks a play start, then the software counts contacts, load per contact and percent of load that is contact (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]). Step 5: add a bioenergetic profile (work time, rest time) and a movement profile (distance and direction per play). From his own season: average play about 8 seconds (7 for a run, 8 for a pass), about 30 seconds between plays for his non-up-tempo offense, about 45 contacts per game, load per contact about 2.12 on passes, 2.32 on runs, 2.22 combined (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10], [06:42], [07:13], [07:45]); the 2.12 caption is garbled ("about two point I'm sorry can you read the two point one two for a pass two point three", [06:42]), so the exact value is uncertain. The caption then reads "they change direction and art plays 25% to the left 25% to the right", which is garbled; it reads as a direction-change figure, not a yardage split, and the exact meaning is unclear. The caption spelling of the position metric is "offensive la Mettrie" (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]), and the passage on what the gyroscope captures "the next five seconds" is garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reason is that total load hides what makes up the load, so the composition has to be measured before practice can be designed (QLdbKUiNadg [03:34], [04:04]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why contact-per-play counts predict injury or performance, and none is claimed. Inference: the value is descriptive. # Define a Lineman's Game Demand by Slicing Each Play and Counting Contacts, Then Train Backwards From It
**What it is** — Chris Morris (University of Kentucky, introduced as the speaker for the sponsor Catapult) describes a method for working out what a position actually does in a game. Step 1: "we train for the demands of the game" and "work our way backwards" (QLdbKUiNadg [02:02]). Step 2: a published study from "a group at the University of Michigan" (a paper he places at about last year) reported about 3,600 yards of game distance, but Morris says that figure is load, not the demands of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [01:32], [03:04]). Step 3: upload every game file to OpenField (Catapult's analytics platform) and "slice each individual play" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). Step 4: use Catapult's offensive-line metric. A gyroscope in the unit recognizes when the lineman drops into his stance, which marks a play start, then the software counts contacts, load per contact and percent of load that is contact (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]). Step 5: add a bioenergetic profile (work time, rest time) and a movement profile (distance and direction per play). From his own season: average play about 8 seconds (7 for a run, 8 for a pass), about 30 seconds between plays for his non-up-tempo offense, about 45 contacts per game, load per contact about 2.12 on passes, 2.32 on runs, 2.22 combined (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10], [06:42], [07:13], [07:45]); the 2.12 caption is garbled ("about two point I'm sorry can you read the two point one two for a pass two point three", [06:42]), so the exact value is uncertain. Work-to-rest was about 1 to 3.75 (QLdbKUiNadg [10:50], [11:21]), and an average play covered 13.5 yards (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). The caption then reads "they change direction and art plays 25% to the left 25% to the right", which is garbled; it reads as a direction-change figure, not a yardage split, and the exact meaning is unclear. The caption spelling of the position metric is "offensive la Mettrie" (QLdbKUiNadg [05:38]), and the passage on what the gyroscope captures "the next five seconds" is garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [06:10]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reason is that total load hides what makes up the load, so the composition has to be measured before practice can be designed (QLdbKUiNadg [03:34], [04:04]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why contact-per-play counts predict injury or performance, and none is claimed. Inference: the value is descriptive. Once a position has a profile (contacts, load per contact, work:rest, yards per play), any practice period can be scored against it.
**When to apply** — When a coach or staff member asks "what does this position need?" and the only available answer is a distance or total-load number. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist" in a formal sense, and Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." Inference: this method is one way to build a position-level profile from Baylor's own Catapult game files, since Baylor already runs Catapult and OpenField.
**When NOT to apply** — One program, one season, one position group (offensive line), and the speaker says he broke down "the thousand plays" from the season (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]), so roughly 1,000 plays from one season. The evidence is a descriptive profile only: the confidence `supported` covers that profile (method plus reported results), not any effect of training to it. The stance-detection metric depends on Catapult hardware and software that the speaker presents on behalf of the vendor, so it is not a vendor-neutral result. The speaker does not show that matching the profile in practice changes performance or injury, and the Q&A (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35] to [15:05]) gives no outcome evidence for it either. The averages (8 seconds, 30 seconds, 45 contacts) belong to Kentucky's offense in his season; an up-tempo offense will differ, as he says himself (QLdbKUiNadg [06:42], [11:21]). Do not import Kentucky's numbers as Baylor targets.
**Example** — From the talk: the average lineman play lasts about 8 seconds and costs a load per contact near 2.22, so the energy-system and contact demand is repeated sub-10-second efforts, and a practice period is judged by how close it gets to that (QLdbKUiNadg [07:45], [10:50]).

# Hold Total Load, Raise Intensity: Trim Low-Value Practice Periods and Ask for Full Speed in the Rest
**What it is** — Asked whether there is evidence that raising practice workload changes game performance or fatigue, the speaker answered with an approach, not evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35], [15:05]):
- "maintain load", control load, "increase our intensity", and prefer shorter, more intense practices (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05]).
- "You can't increase the intensity and volume" together "because then you create massive amounts of fatigue"; wellness questionnaires help judge internal load next to external load (QLdbKUiNadg [15:35]).
- Camp example: in a three-hour practice a skill player may cover about 7,000 yards but "he's just gonna pace", at "1718 miles an hour" (caption; read as 17 to 18 mph in the summary; a second caption, "around 218 miles an hour", is also garbled). The quarterback's timing is then off when receivers move faster in a game (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05], [15:35]).
- With wide receivers, the compromise was to pull back seven-on-seven blitz-package periods where they were "just running routes for no reason", so they run full speed in the remaining seven-on-seven and team periods, with load unchanged (QLdbKUiNadg [18:08]).
- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance during the week (QLdbKUiNadg [13:27]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that athletes pace themselves when practice is long, so the pace they learn is not the pace of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05]). The claim that both volume and intensity cannot rise without fatigue is stated as fact without evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [15:35]). Inference: this is a restatement of constant-load, higher-intensity redistribution and relies on external load (GPS) staying equal while the mix changes.
**When to apply** — In camp or in-season when practices run long and speed is low per period. Eric's baseline: the HHPR 5355 course material states the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21`), tagged Inferred (course-team speaker unconfirmed). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps." Inference: the speaker's version adds the practical lever (cut low-value periods, name the intensity expected in the rest).
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's assertion and one camp example. The questioner asked for evidence and the answer gave an approach, with no outcome data (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35], [15:05]). The 17 to 18 mph figure is a caption problem and implausible as a sustained pace; do not quote it. The "75% of game high-speed distance" target is Kentucky's for skill players, not a validated number. Athlete buy-in matters, as the speaker's Eagles anecdote shows (players pushed back on doing more work, QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]; see the related entry).
**Example** — The wide-receiver compromise above: fewer seven-on-seven blitz-pack reps, full speed in the ones that remain, unchanged load (QLdbKUiNadg [18:08]).

# If a Coach Ignores the Report, Change the Question, Then Show Athletes Their Own Data
**What it is** — Three episodes from Morris's talk:
- **The trashed report.** He put a report he was "really proud of" on the offensive-line coach's desk and the coach threw it in the trash (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). His first reaction was that he had a PhD and was the expert; he then concluded that the coach told him "you're not having the right conversation," and he asks whether his data was; "in that case it wasn't" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]).
- **The reframe.** The coach said he wanted to see "how much they're bangin and practice" (caption) (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]). Morris answered by first measuring the game (about 45 contacts, load per contact about 2.22) so the practice figures were comparable (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13], [07:45]).
- **Athlete buy-in.** Athletes must be "connected" to their data internally and externally, "because if you don't they don't have a lot of buy-in they feel like lab rats" (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]). He mentions an earlier case, the Eagles under Chip Kelly, where, he says, players pushed back on being made to do more work (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]).
He also notes that coaches grade in subjective terms, and without objective data a dispute is "just your opinion versus my opinion" (QLdbKUiNadg [01:02], [01:32]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the report answered a question the coach was not asking. He gives no evidence beyond his own experience. Inference: a coach's own question (here, contact in practice versus game) gets attention, while a generic report does not.
**When to apply** — When a coach does not read or use a report. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: the coach's question is the "where to look", and the data answer it. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams." Inference: at Baylor the person who reframes the report for the coach is often the strength staff member.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: anecdote, a single coach, a single athlete group. The talk does not report whether the reframed reports changed decisions or results. It does not support using data to win arguments with a coach; the speaker describes the reverse (first reaction: "you should listen to me", QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]). The Eagles reference is a second-hand recollection by the speaker.
**Example** — The talk's own: the practice-versus-game contact comparison was built because the line coach wanted to see "how much they're bangin" (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]).

# SSAC19: Analytics for the Front Office: Valuing Protections on NBA Draft Picks  Captions: YouTube auto-generated (en). Expect misspelled names and jargon.  
[00:00] Hello. Hey everyone, good afternoon. Uh welcome to the research papers presentations presented by MLB. Um today we're going to have Benjamin Foster of UNC um talk about analytics for the front office, valuing protections on NBA draft picks. Uh the presentation will be 20 minutes and then we'll have 5 minutes for a Q&A. Uh so please help me in welcoming Benjamin. Thanks, Jonah. Um I'm glad they served  
[00:31] you guys sandwiches before this talk, so I'm not standing between you and lunch. Um if this doesn't work, my co-author is back there to save me. There we go. Um so uh like Jonah said, I'm Ben Foster, I'm a PhD student actually in environmental sciences and engineering. Um and I'm going to talk about our work where we take some theories um and methods from financial asset pricing um and try to use those to produce a value of protecting NBA draft picks. When I say value, I don't mean monetary value. I mean basketball value, so in some term  
[01:02] of player uh value or player value metric. So I want to make that clear up front. Um and my again, my co-author Michael Bins uh is here. Um he's a consultant at North Highland um in Philadelphia. So uh uh we're interested in in doing this because draft picks are important assets in the trade market, and that's why we use player value because often they're used uh to trade for players. Um and I'll bring in the most prolific trader of NBA draft picks Ted Stepyien to help me uh give you a little uh background here.  
[01:32] Um so a draft pick is a colloquial term uh that the NBA more uh precisely defines as a right to make a draft choice. I will use draft pick throughout this talk, um but I wanted to make that clear up front. Um and each year every team gets this right um in both rounds of the NBA draft. Of course, it's not tied to a particular draft slot, what we call a pick position. And that's determined after the season as a function of standings and a lottery process for those top 14 picks.  
[02:02] Okay, so teams uh as I mentioned can trade their first round draft picks, although there are some restrictions on that now thanks to our friend Ted. Um but what is most interesting, I think, is that when they trade those draft picks, they're allowed to add something called protections to the draft picks. So these are conditions on the transfer of the draft pick based on its pick predict pick position. And the easiest way to understand these is through an example. Um and we'll we'll use this throughout the talk. So this is the Lakers 2015 first round pick. It was initially traded to the Suns for Steve Nash in  
[02:33] 2012. It was then traded from the Suns to the Sixers in 2015 at the trade deadline. So that's the kind of reference point is that 2015 trade deadline. I think I'm feeding back. I'll move over here. Uh but that pick was protected top five in 2015, uh which means if the Lakers were to end up with the first, second, third, fourth, or fifth pick, they would get to keep it. The Sixers in this case would not get the pick that year. It would roll over. Oh, this is a conundrum. It works when I'm over here, but then I feed back. Um uh it would roll over to the next uh  
[03:05] years where it was top three protected for a couple years, then unprotected in 2018. So we call this combination of things a the base draft pick, the Lakers 2015 first round pick, plus its protection scheme a draft pick asset. And this is the thing we're interested in analyzing. All right. My co-author is back there, and I think I'm just going to flag him to switch uh slots. So uh what are the benefits of protections? To understand that, uh we need to understand uh what a base draft  
[03:36] pick looks like. Um and it looks like a distribution of possible pick position outcomes. So at some point in the middle of the year, you're uncertain how you're going to finish, you're uncertain the results of the draft lottery. And so this is what your pick posi- or your draft pick looks like. If you were to trade it, you'd be giving a team this set of probable outcomes. Um and so if we uh think about this in a trade context, this has a single value. You could trade this for for something, teams would evaluate it with one single value. But if you add protections, you can change  
[04:07] the distribution of picks. Um so this is one protection scheme. Uh we've got a couple more uh coming here. Um and you can do this a bunch of different ways. It turns out there actually millions of ways to do this. Um uh of protection schemes, which means you can take that base draft pick and give it millions of different values in a uh as a trade asset. So uh why this is uh particularly valuable um is that the uh trading in the NBA is a difficult thing to do. Um there's lots of reasons why. Um it's a  
[04:37] barter system, there's lots of restrictions from the NBA um in part of the bylaws and in the CBA. There's a good reason to do this from but from a market efficiency standpoint, we would say that this is a really illiquid market. It's very difficult to make transactions, to buy and sell when you want to buy and sell at market rates. Um and so uh but pick protections are this one thing that appears uh or ought to increase the likelihood of a transaction occurring. So if you imagine you're a team uh Oh. It's flying through. Okay. If you  
[05:07] imagine you're a team uh and you're uh trying to trade for some medium value asset, but you only hold very high value and very low value assets, it might be very difficult for you to assemble a package uh that will make that transaction occur. Uh with pick protections, you can take some of those high or low value assets, raise or lower their value, increasing the likelihood you might be able to execute a trade. Um so of course teams understand this um and they use pick protections all the time. Um this was uh figure that we first started this project looking at. Um it  
[05:38] was really the motivation. We've kind of updated a couple times since, but uh this is picks traded from 2011 to 2017, their level of protection across the x-axis, and the number of picks across the y. And you'll notice uh that there's these three kind of clusters. That's top five protected, top 10 protected, and top 14 protected. Um we found this quite interesting, right? If teams are using protections to tailor the value of a draft pick to particular trade circumstances, it's quite odd that lots and lots of trade circumstances require  
[06:08] a top 10 protection as opposed to top nine or top 11, where there's actually only one top 11 protection in this data set. Um and so we thought maybe there ought to be a more smooth distribution. And our hypothesis for why this situation might be the case is that teams have a difficult time quantifying uh precisely, at least, the difference between, say, top nine, top 10, and top 11. As a result, you end up on a round number. We call these psychological anchors in the paper. So we have five and 10 and 14 as a basketball number, uh which we call a round number here.  
[06:39] So uh we thought about, well, could we come up with a way to calculate the value or the difference between, say, a top nine versus a top 10 protection, top 11 versus top 14? And this motivates our primary research question, uh which is how valuable are pick protections on NBA draft picks. And our strategy for answering this question is to build out a system that can value systematically value draft picks with any protection scheme. We call this price. And as I mentioned before, this is a basketball price, so that we're not confused uh  
[07:09] that we're going to think about money here. Um okay, and our purpose, before we get into some of the methods, I want to remind uh keep this at the forefront of your mind, is to help inform team decision-making about where you might place protections. So could you better decide how to protect a pick when you trade it away, or how to protect a pick when you're trading for it? Okay, so uh the basis of our modeling is this insight that protected draft picks are like financial options. So if you imagine a world in which you just want to write down how will what is  
[07:40] the value of a draft pick asset, you might say, well, it's going to be a function of the protections, this contractual artifact um of the the draft pick asset, and that draft pick's future position. So what we really care about here is the volatility of that position, right? How probable is it that it will fall within or outside of the protections? This turns out parallels pretty closely to how we think about option value, so financial option value. Um there's a strike, which we don't need to know the details of, but is analogous to protections, is a contractual artifact. Um and then the underlying asset's  
[08:10] future value. Again, we care about the volatility of that future value. Um that is the likelihood, for example, that it might exceed the strike value. So Nobel prizes have been awarded for describing the mathematics behind these option value formulas. I don't think there will be one awarded for describing the the mathematics behind draft pick asset values. But uh we also don't want to use the math directly. It applies very specifically to these types of assets. Um so we use kind of the principles that underlie that math and  
[08:40] adapt them with our own uh methods uh to to price out these draft picks. So these are kind of broadly the three principles that we use. Uh we first characterize the volatility in the underlying asset, um then assess the impact of the contractual conditions, there's a protections, um and then account for market risk to boil that all down into a single price or single value. This is what our system looks like. Um we've got, and this is roughly how they fit into those three uh principles. Um  
[09:10] these gray boxes here contain a lot of details. You can find them in the paper, you can find them on our poster, um but I'm going to try to keep it relatively high level. If I'd started here, you guys would have all left 5 minutes ago. Um but the important piece here are these are these are these first two modules um or that they describe two sources of uncertainty uh that we're worried about. So the first is where will a team finish in the standings? And the way we model this is using an ELO rating system-based model that simulates an an NBA season, um and  
[09:40] allows us to estimate the probability distribution of the team's ultimate standings position. Now this is inverse for us, so when we say one, that means the worst team in the league. This lines up better with how picks are are dealt out. Um so I'll I'll bring it back to that Lakers 2015 pick. At the trade deadline. We simulate the 20 or or so odd games left for every NBA team. We do that 10,000 times and end up with this distribution of possible finishing positions for the Lakers. Okay, so the second module here is pick  
[10:11] position valuation. This is trying to account for how valuable a player could be picked at any position. Right, the first pick you can end up with Anthony Bennett or LeBron James. We might want to capture that variability. And we do so by building out these cumulative probability distributions. In our case, we use win shares. It's simple to interpret. You could use whatever metric you want here, proprietary metrics, PER, whatever you think is important. But the important piece is to be able to build these cumulative probability dis distributions.  
[10:42] And we did so using historic data from Basketball-Reference. We indexed it by pick position, so when the player was picked, and that's how we built them out. So, of course here we've got Tim Duncan and LeBron James at the far end of this curve, and Anthony Bennett's down low, and Andrew Bogut falls about there on this distribution. And we can do this for every pick. So, we do it every pick out to pick 30. We're we're just worried about the first round here. And that's in bright red. Okay, so we've captured the uncertainty in these two modules at the top here.  
[11:14] And we feed that into a Monte Carlo simulation. We run that 10,000 times, and this is where we account for lottery probabilities and protection schemes. I'll give you the very coarse overview of what goes on here. We start with that output from module one. And we feed that through the way we account for draft lotteries and the protection scheme. Combine that with the output from module two, and the result is this value generated by pick assets. So, this is the important piece right here. I'll actually blow this up and  
[11:45] look at it in more detail. So, this is win shares over the first five years of a player's career. I think I forgot to mention that. We sum win shares over the first five years of their career. This is our player value metric that we're interested in. And it's the those win shares simulated win shares generated by the specific pick asset. So, that Lakers pick with its protections. And to interpret this, you might say, "Okay, this bar here represents a 16.8% chance that the Sixers, in this case, who own  
[12:16] this pick, would be able to draft a player with it who contributes between 17 and a half and 21 and a half win shares over their first five years." Okay, so that's the main output from this Monte Carlo simulation, and that feeds into our financial asset pricing model. So, the goal here is to take that distribution of outcomes and boil it down into a single value. And I'll do that in two I'll show how we do this with two distributions. So, this is that protected pick that we've been  
[12:46] talking about. And I'll also show a counterfactual, which is the unprotected 2015 Lakers pick. So, this doesn't exist cuz they traded that protected pick, but we can compare the two and estimate how valuable protections were by doing this. So, the first way you might think about boiling this distribution down is to take the expected value or the mean of this distribution. So, that those are the black lines there, but the issue is that doesn't account for the variance in the distribution. And you might care about that because these really big outcomes here  
[13:17] are the result of picks one through three, which essentially get ruled out of this protected case because of the protections. This is the chance of getting LeBron James or someone who might change your your franchise's history. So, you might want to weight that a little bit when you assess the the the value of this pick. To do that, we use something called the Wang transform. It's a financial asset pricing model that we use because it works very well for empirical distributions. And it just has a single assumption, which is called the market price of  
[13:47] risk. And this is the math, but the important piece here is this highlighted gamma value. This is that one assumption. It's can be represented as the sharp ratio, which is something you can calculate if you're worried about stocks or corporate bonds or something heavily traded instruments. You can calculate this. But we're interested in the more general interpretation of the market price of risk, which is can be understood kind of generally as the risk preferences of the  
[14:18] market. So, now we need to figure out how the NBA trade market values different draft pick positions. We don't think that they should or they probably don't treat pick one like they treat pick 30. And so, our solution for this problem was to go back to our module two output. So, remember this is player performance cumulative probability distributions. We use K-means clustering, too. And a filtering method, and we identify like assets. So, we end up with seven distinct asset classes that Michael will flip through here.  
[14:48] And then we assign a different market price of risk for each of those asset classes. We have calibrated these using pick-for-picks trades. There aren't very many of those. More work could be done here to calibrate these values. But we calibrated them, we interpolated when we needed to, and these were the the values we came up with. So, to interpret this, pick one is all by itself, and we have a very risk-seeking market price of risk. So, that means teams are willing to pay much more than the expected value. And then for pick 25 and 30, it's very  
[15:19] risk-averse parameter. So, teams are willing to pay less than the values. So, I will say that hopefully that aligns with your intuition. When you hear about the trade, you often hear about teams taking risks at pick one, going for upside. At pick 25 and 30, they're looking for role players. They're interested in kind of their base contribution. Okay, so the result we put this all into this Wang transform model. We use this distribution, we end up with these yellow lines.  
[15:49] So, you'll notice in the unprotected case, that yellow line is way out to the right. So, that tail of that distribution pulled the price way out. In the protected case, it's actually relatively close to that expected value. And these are our prices, right? So, it's 43.1 win shares per five years and 21.0. To give you a little more context, you can break that out into a kind of a implied annual win share contribution. It's 8.6 here, which is 2018 Kemba Walker in the unprotected case. In the protected case, it's 2018 Tyler Johnson.  
[16:20] So, for some of you that will be meaningful and help you understand this. Um The So, the other thing we can do, I mentioned this is kind of a counterfactual situation. Excuse me. Um And we can compare the two and then say the protection subtracted about 51% of the value of the pick of that base draft pick. So, I will talk about this a little bit more, but I want to back up and give you some context to the trade that this pick was involved in. So, it was the Suns-Sixers-Bucks trade. And the  
[16:51] Suns traded away that Lakers first-round pick in exchange for Brandon Knight and Kendall Marshall, who they ended up waving I think immediately. So, we'll compare these two. And at the time this Lakers pick was perceived to be a pretty high-value asset. A lot of folks were asking this question, and it's interesting to see Ryan McDonough, who's the GM of the Suns at the time, his response to this question. So, he says, "With a pick like that, we probably weren't going to receive the pick this year." And this lines up with our model findings. So, we end up assessing there's a 78% chance that that  
[17:22] pick was going to end up protected in that first year. So, he goes on and says, "Well, that pushes it back next year, and there's a pretty high variance as to what the Lakers how what pick what the pick could be." And that also lines up with our model. So, the Lakers were fourth the fourth worst team at the time. Suppose they were to finish fourth worst. We estimated the distribution of outcomes the next year was first worst and 24th worst, so sixth best. The median outcome there was eight. And he concludes and says, "If you ask  
[17:52] me how the Lakers are going to be a year from now, I have no idea." It kind of sounds like the uncertainty was a driving force in this trade. Getting rid of this pick. And we can go back and kind of think about what return they got, at least on this one dimension. So, like I said that we priced that protected pick at 4.2 win shares. Brandon Knight, who they got in return, had generated around 4.5 in the previous year and was on track for the same in 2015. So, there's a lot going on there. Uh  
[18:22] Brandon Knight was Go back a couple. Okay. Brandon Knight was um about to be a free agent. There's team-building considerations. There's all sorts of considerations. But this is another piece of data I think to use to analyze possibly past trades or prospective trades. So, we've got a bunch of other results that you can find in the paper, on the poster. We don't have time to go through them too much here. But one is this Bucks-Suns trade. There's the Eric Bledsoe trade in November 2017. The  
[18:53] interesting thing there is the are these low-end protections, so 17 through 30. That does some interesting things to the value. Hopefully, if we are fortunate enough to have the opportunity to talk tomorrow, we'll input some of this discussion into that talk. And then we answer a couple other questions, like what's the value of incremental protections or multiple-year protections. So, we call this rollover protections. So, for a few discussion points, we've used these quantitative methods hopefully to say something about what  
[19:23] the value of um NBA draft picks are, protected NBA draft picks are. But I think there's a few ways we can improve our model, and we built it kind of modularly, so we can update methods over time. So, the first thing, there's a bunch here. I'll just mention two. One is that the team simulation doesn't really account for player movement right now. There are updated methods that could be used. We had some We're working on this project on the side and using personal computers, and so we had some computing constraints and time constraints. But we can implement more sophisticated methods here to account for when a team trades a  
[19:55] player away, they might get worse, they might get better, um but there might be a jump in their performance, and we don't account for that currently. Um and then uh I mentioned this in the talk, better calibrating those risk preference parameters um could be done uh with some updated methods. The other thing we'd like to do is add some customizability to the the model. Um if this is going to be used by teams as private information to make decisions about pick protections, they may want to input their own risk preferences, expectations about draft quality or  
[20:25] future team performance, or choose a new or different player value metric. Um and those uh updates may not aren't going to be that difficult, I think, to add in here. Um so we've mentioned some of these applications. Um we could analyze past trades, which is what we've kind of done here today. Um we call this kind of tongue-in-cheek advanced analytics of the front office. The idea there is the front office has had their chance to advance analyze players and coaches, and maybe it's their turn under the microscope. Um the second uh would be private information. So this is allowing teams to better negotiate  
[20:56] pick protections um or perhaps target mispriced assets. That's an arbitrage argument that might be hard to make in a market that's like the NBA trade market and is a liquid, but um it still may be possible. Um and then the third is a more general idea, a larger a cons- conceptual idea, and that's to use this framework of NBA assets as financial assets um and try to price out or value other asset types, things like bird rights or draft and stash decisions um might be able to be maneuvered into this  
[21:26] framework. And that's it. If you have any questions Oh, my co-author's a Duke fan, and I went to Virginia, so I had the opportunity here to put a bunch of Virginia players scoring on Duke. Um so that's why this is up here. We can now open up for questions.  
[21:56] I think maybe you had a follow-up point on it that would be relevant to it, but did you do anything with discounting rates for the player performance? I mean, the front office is a big consideration that's like, "Well, you know, I'm I may not be the person to make that pick." So um so there's there was that piece, and then also um the flip side value of, you know, the the draft pick, as they say, it's you know, it's eventually becomes a player, and if that player isn't the player another team likes, it's not as valuable as the pick that was taken to get it. And so there would maybe some future option value to the pick actually rolling over um so that you can continue to keep it  
[22:26] as a more of a financial asset rather than a realized asset. Yeah. Yeah, there are lots of time considerations here, lots of dimensions that we don't deal with, in part because it's kind of hard for me to think about, kind of from a market perspective, whether assets are more valuable now or later. It's not like money.
