# Case Study: The Lakers 2015 Pick and What Its Protection Was Worth
**What it is** — Benjamin Foster prices the Lakers 2015 first-round pick, protected top five in 2015, and compares it with an unprotected counterfactual that never existed (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46]).
- **Prices.** 43.1 win shares per five years unprotected and 21.0 protected; the implied annual value for the unprotected case is 8.6, which he equates to 2018 Kemba Walker, and the protected case to 2018 Tyler Johnson (SIn6IyYQEVI [15:49]). He says the protection subtracted about 51 percent of the base pick's value (SIn6IyYQEVI [16:20]). Context: one output bar showed a 16.8 percent chance of a player with between 17.5 and 21.5 win shares (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:45], [12:16]).
- **The trade.** The Suns traded the pick to the Sixers in a Suns-Sixers-Bucks deal for Brandon Knight and Kendall Marshall (SIn6IyYQEVI [16:20], [16:51]).
- **Check against the GM's comments.** The Suns general manager (named in captions as Ryan McDonough) said they probably would not receive the pick that year; the model gave a 78 percent chance it would be protected in the first year (SIn6IyYQEVI [16:51], [17:22]). He also said the pick's later position was highly uncertain; the model, assuming the Lakers finished fourth worst, gave a range from worst to 24th worst the next year, median eight (SIn6IyYQEVI [17:22]).
- **Return received.** The protected pick priced at "4.2 win shares" (as spoken; he does not say per year. Inference: 21.0 divided by five is 4.2, so it is probably the annual figure), against about 4.5 that Knight had produced the previous year and was on track for in 2015 (SIn6IyYQEVI [17:52], [18:22]).
Other cases in the paper (the Bucks-Suns trade, the Eric Bledsoe trade in November 2017 with protections on 17 to 30) are named but not worked through (SIn6IyYQEVI [18:22], [18:53]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's reading is that uncertainty about the Lakers' future "was a driving force" in the trade, based on the GM's quote (SIn6IyYQEVI [17:52]). He does not claim the model proves intent.
**When to apply** — As a template for reviewing a past transaction using only what was knowable at the time: price the asset, compare to what came back, list what the model leaves out. Inference: the same retrospective applies to a past scholarship or portal decision. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one trade, one model, no outside check on the price beyond the GM's quotes (which he says line up). The comparison omits that Knight was about to be a free agent and other team-building factors, which the speaker says himself (SIn6IyYQEVI [18:22]). Inference: the 4.2 versus 4.5 comparison mixes a projected per-year average over five years with one player's single season. Treat 51 percent as the model's output for this pick, not a general discount for protections.
**Example** — The speaker's own, above.
**Related** — [[framework--price-a-protected-draft-pick-like-a-financial-option]]; [[principle--value-an-uncertain-asset-by-its-outcome-distribution-not-its-mean]].

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster (with co-author Michael Bins, caption spelling) prices a draft pick plus its protection scheme (a "draft pick asset") in player-value terms, not money (SIn6IyYQEVI [00:31], [01:02], [03:05]). A protection is a condition that lets the trading team keep the pick if it lands in a protected range, with the pick rolling over to later years (the Lakers 2015 pick was top-5 protected in 2015, top-3 for a couple of years, then unprotected in 2018) (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:02] to [03:05]). The analogy is a financial option: the protection plays the part of the contract terms, and the volatility of the underlying value matters (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40], [08:10]). He does not use the option math directly, only its principles (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:10], [08:40]). Three steps (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]):
1. **Characterize volatility of the underlying asset.** Module one: an Elo-rating season simulation that gives a distribution of finishing position (1 means worst, to match how picks are dealt), run 10,000 times over the roughly 20 remaining games at the trade deadline (SIn6IyYQEVI [09:10], [09:40]). Module two: cumulative distributions of player value by pick position, using Basketball-Reference history for first-round picks, with win shares as the metric (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [10:42]).
2. **Assess the contract conditions.** A 10,000-run Monte Carlo combines lottery probabilities and the protection scheme into a distribution of win shares summed over a player's first five years (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:14], [11:45]).
3. **Account for market risk** with a Wang transform (see [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]]), reducing the distribution to a single price (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:16], [13:17]).
He states the purpose is to help a team decide where to place protections when trading a pick away or trading for one (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:09]). Because millions of protection schemes exist, one base pick can have millions of trade values (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). The model is modular, so the player value metric can be swapped (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [19:23]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the option parallel: how likely the pick is to fall inside versus outside the protected range drives value (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40]). He gives no tested argument that this transfer from finance is accurate; he says they adapt the principles "with our own methods" (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]).
**When to apply** — As a template for any asset that arrives as an uncertain outcome with contract conditions: model the uncertainty source, apply the conditions in simulation, then price. Inference: for Baylor, the closest analogs are recruiting and portal classes (an uncertain future player value) rather than any monitoring work; the applications note flags low direct use for Applied Performance. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one worked example (see [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]]), calibration from few pick-for-pick trades, and no outcome test. # Value an Uncertain Asset by Its Whole Outcome Distribution, Not Its Mean
**What it is** — Benjamin Foster argues that a mean hides the spread of an asset's outcomes. A base draft pick "looks like a distribution of possible pick position outcomes," so trading it gives the other team that set of outcomes (SIn6IyYQEVI [03:36]). A protection changes the distribution, not just its center (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). Taking the mean "doesn't account for the variance," and the extreme outcomes (picks one through three, the chance of getting LeBron James or "someone who might change your franchise's history") are exactly what protection removes, so the model weights them (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46], [13:17]). In the unprotected case the priced value sits far to the right of the mean because of the tail; in the protected case the price is "relatively close to the expected value" (SIn6IyYQEVI [15:49]). The tool is a risk adjustment (the Wang transform) with a market price of risk (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [13:47]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is that teams care about outcomes in the tails, and the market prices that preference (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [14:18]). He gives no empirical test that the adjustment is correct.
**When to apply** — When comparing options with different spreads (a high-ceiling prospect versus a safe contributor): show the range of outcomes in one unit, then say which end the decision values. Inference: a recruiting board could express each prospect as best, typical and worst case in one unit and compare classes by spread, as the applications note proposes. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker presents a method and one worked example with no validation, and the risk parameter is calibrated on few pick-for-pick trades (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48]). If decision makers value only the average, or the outcome data are too thin to build a distribution (small samples at one position), a distribution adds false precision. The adjustment depends on the assumed market risk preference, which is a stated assumption, not a measurement.
**Example** — The speaker's own: the protected and unprotected versions of the same pick (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46], [15:49]); the numbers are in [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]].

# Case Study: The Lakers 2015 Pick and What Its Protection Was Worth

He says the protection subtracted about 51 percent of the base pick's value (SIn6IyYQEVI [16:20]). Context: one output bar showed a 16.8 percent chance of a player with between 17.5 and 21.5 win shares (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:45], [12:16]).
- **The trade.** The Suns traded the pick to the Sixers in a Suns-Sixers-Bucks deal for Brandon Knight and Kendall Marshall (SIn6IyYQEVI [16:20], [16:51]).
- **Check against the GM's comments.** The Suns general manager (named in captions as Ryan McDonough) said they probably would not receive the pick that year; the model gave a 78 percent chance it would be protected in the first year (SIn6IyYQEVI [16:51], [17:22]). - **Return received.** The protected pick priced at "4.2 win shares" (as spoken; he does not say per year. Other cases in the paper (the Bucks-Suns trade, the Eric Bledsoe trade in November 2017 with protections on 17 to 30) are named but not worked through (SIn6IyYQEVI [18:22], [18:53]).
**Why it works** — The speaker's reading is that uncertainty about the Lakers' future "was a driving force" in the trade, based on the GM's quote (SIn6IyYQEVI [17:52]). He does not claim the model proves intent.
**When to apply** — As a template for reviewing a past transaction using only what was knowable at the time: price the asset, compare to what came back, list what the model leaves out. Inference: the same retrospective applies to a past scholarship or portal decision. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one trade, one model, no outside check on the price beyond the GM's quotes (which he says line up). The comparison omits that Knight was about to be a free agent and other team-building factors, which the speaker says himself (SIn6IyYQEVI [18:22]). Inference: the 4.2 versus 4.5 comparison mixes a projected per-year average over five years with one player's single season. Treat 51 percent as the model's output for this pick, not a general discount for protections.

# Traded Draft-Pick Protections Cluster at Top 5, Top 10 and Top 14
**What it is** — Benjamin Foster shows a figure of picks traded from 2011 to 2017 by level of protection, with three clusters: top-five, top-10 and top-14 protected (SIn6IyYQEVI [05:38]). It is odd, the speaker says, that so many trades need a top-10 protection rather than top nine or top 11, where only one top-11 protection is in the data set (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]). The counts are on a slide and are not read out. The speaker's hypothesis is that teams cannot easily quantify the difference between top nine, 10 and 11, so they land on round numbers, which the paper calls "psychological anchors" (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]). This motivated the research question: could one calculate the value difference between, say, top nine and top 10 (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:39]). The speaker also says protections raise the chance a trade happens: teams that hold only very high- or very low-value assets can adjust them to assemble a package for a medium-value target in an illiquid barter market (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:37], [05:07]). The speaker says the pick position is set by standings and a lottery for the top 14 picks (SIn6IyYQEVI [01:32]).
**Why it works** — The anchoring explanation is a hypothesis ("our hypothesis for why this situation might be the case"), not tested (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]). The transaction-ease point is the speaker's expectation: protections "appear or ought to" raise the likelihood of a transaction (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:37]).
**When to apply** — As a prompt: where decision rules cluster at round numbers (cutoffs, thresholds, tiers), ask whether the number comes from analysis or from anchoring. Inference: this fits any staff cutoff that sits at 5, 10 or a round percentile. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.
**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the pattern is a descriptive figure over seven seasons of one league, the cause is a hypothesis, and the underlying counts are not in the transcript. Inference: round-number clustering could also reflect conventions among negotiators; the talk does not test this. Do not generalize beyond NBA protected picks.
**Example** — The speaker's own: a top-10 protection chosen far more often than top-nine or top-11 (SIn6IyYQEVI [06:08]).

The averages (8 seconds, 30 seconds, 45 contacts) belong to Kentucky's offense in his season; an up-tempo offense will differ, as he says himself (QLdbKUiNadg [06:42], [11:21]). Do not import Kentucky's numbers as Baylor targets.

**Example** — From the talk: the average lineman play lasts about 8 seconds and costs a load per contact near 2.22, so the energy-system and contact demand is repeated sub-10-second efforts, and a practice period is judged by how close it gets to that (QLdbKUiNadg [07:45], [10:50]).
